<reason>Both sides were strong, but A won the decisive exchanges. A's construction-cost vs operating-cost distinction forced B to concede that a sustainably operable network can rationally go unbuilt, undermining "carrier refusal = information about worth." A's pressure question on vouchers exposed that B's demand-side alternative cannot create missing supply, and B's reply leaned on "credibly arriving" service—a forecast B demanded rigor from A but not from himself. A answered both pressure questions directly and cleanly (A4.1-A4.3), while B's A1 partially dodged by narrowing vouchers to "almost everywhere." A also read the motion faithfully: "even when" non-viable is not "whenever carriers say so," and refusal is itself forecast-based. B's sharpest line—appraisal disciplines fraud, not error, and government forecasts replace market measurement—survived as a live route and was well-delivered, but A's demanding-threshold-with-conservative-valuation reply, plus the symmetry point that all public spending (schools, clinics) rests on unpriced benefits, kept B from converting it into a winning burden. B's residual position ("the connection may not justify its cost") quietly concedes the principle A defends. Narrow but clear edge to A on directness, burden handling, and motion fidelity, despite B's superior punchiness.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question [A3.1] and the follow-through in [A4.4]: if subscriptions cover maintenance but not construction, vouchers either fail or become construction subsidies themselves—forcing B into the concession at [B4.1] and the weaker counter at [B4.2]. B's best counterpunch was [B4.5]-[B4.6]: appraisal screens for fraud, not error, since the thing appraised is what carriers already measured.</best_rebuttal>
